1:9.headline: Was Saul seized by trembling, or caught in his armor?
1:9.body: השבץ usually is read as a fit of trembling that took hold of the dying Saul. Ralbag reads it instead as his woven armor, which stopped the spear from going in, and a midrash links the word to the woven tunic of the priests Saul had killed.

sources.quote: מִשּׁוּם עָוֹן הַכֹּהֲנִים שֶׁהָרַג, וְכָתוּב בָּהֶן
sources.says: Rashi gives the Targum's 'trembling seized me', then a midrash that it came for the sin of the priests Saul killed, who wore a 'כתנת תשבץ', a woven tunic.

sources.quote: שהלבוש שהיה לבוש היה משובץ להוסיף לו חוזק
sources.says: Ralbag thinks Saul's garment was woven to make it strong, so the spear he fell on could not pierce it.

1:18.headline: Real archery lessons, or the bow as a sign of strength?
1:18.body: David says to teach Judah the bow. Ralbag reads it as real training, since Saul fell to archers. Radak reads the bow as a picture of military strength that belongs to Judah.

sources.quote: בעבור שראה כי מיתת שאול היתה בסבת יראתו מהמורים בקשת
sources.says: Ralbag says David saw that Saul died out of fear of the archers, so he wanted Judah trained in the bow.

sources.quote: ובאמרו קשת כי הוא עיקר כלי המלחמה ודרך הכתוב לזכור במקום זכר גבורה
sources.says: Radak says the bow is named because it is the main weapon, and Scripture uses it to stand for might.

1:18.headline: The 'Book of the Upright' is read as Genesis
1:18.body: ספר הישר means 'the book of the upright'. Rashi says it is Genesis, the book of the upright fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The Targum calls it the book of the Torah.

sources.quote: שֶׁהִיא סֵפֶר יְשָׁרִים, אַבְרָהָם יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב
sources.says: Rashi says the book is Genesis, called upright after the patriarchs, and finds the bow hinted in Jacob's blessing to Judah.

sources.quote: עַל סִפְרָא דְאוֹרַיְתָא
sources.says: The Targum translates it as 'the book of the Torah'.

1:19.headline: 'The beauty of Israel' or 'you who stood firm'?
1:19.body: הצבי can mean the glory or the desired land, so the lament opens by calling to the Land of Israel. The Targum reads it from the root for standing, as in the place where Israel's fighters stood.

sources.quote: ארץ ישראל קרויה ארץ צבי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the Land of Israel is called the land of צבי, a word for beauty and desire, and the ה is a call, 'O beauty'.

sources.quote: פי' הצבי מענין נצב נצבים
sources.says: Radak explains the Targum as reading הצבי from נצב, to stand.

sources.quote: מַצְבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi follows the Targum: the station of Israel, the strong place where they fell.

1:21.headline: The shield was despised, or it spat out its oil
1:21.body: נגעל usually means despised or cast off. Rashi reads it as 'spat out': the leather shield would not hold the oil rubbed on it, as if it was never oiled.

sources.quote: ענין מאוס ותעוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means loathed, as in 'my soul will loathe you'.

sources.quote: כָּל ׳הַגְעָלָה׳ לְשׁוֹן דָּבָר הַפּוֹלֵט מַה שֶּׁנּוֹתְנִין בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says this root always means something that spits out what is put into it, so the shield shed its oil.

1:21.headline: An unoiled shield, or a king no longer anointed?
1:21.body: בלי משיח בשמן, 'not anointed with oil', may describe the shield, which soldiers oiled before battle. It may also describe Saul himself, the anointed king, fallen as if he had never been anointed.

sources.quote: או פירושו כן נגעל כאילו לא היה שאול משוח בשמן למלך
sources.says: Radak gives both readings: the shield as if never oiled, or Saul as if never anointed king.

1:24.headline: A midrash reads 'daughters of Israel' as its courts of sages
1:24.body: Plainly the daughters of Israel weep because Saul fed and clothed them. One sage in a midrash reads them as Israel's courts of scholars, whom Saul honored.

sources.quote: ר' נחמיה אומר בנות ישראל אלו סנהדראות של ישראל
sources.says: Radak brings a midrash where Rabbi Yehuda reads real women and Rabbi Nehemiah reads the courts of sages, since Saul kissed a scholar who gave a good reason for a law.

1:24.headline: Delicacies to eat, or fine clothes to wear?
1:24.body: עדנים means things that pamper. The Targum takes it as food Saul brought the women. Radak says it can also mean fine clothing, which pampers the body as good food does.

sources.quote: וּמוֹבִיל לְכוֹן תַּפְנוּקִין
sources.says: The Targum translates 'and brought you delicacies'.

sources.quote: ויש לפרשו כמשמעו כי הלבוש הטוב והנאה עדן הגוף כמו המאכל הטוב
sources.says: Radak says it can be read plainly: fine clothing is a delight to the body like good food.

1:26.headline: A doubled feminine ending makes the wonder stronger
1:26.body: נפלאתה, 'was wonderful', carries two feminine endings where one is enough. Radak says the doubling stresses how wonderful Jonathan's love was.

sources.quote: בשני סימני נקיבה והכפל לחזק פליאת האהבה
sources.says: Radak says the word has two feminine markers and the doubling strengthens the wonder of the love.

1:26.headline: Which 'love of women' did Jonathan's love surpass?
1:26.body: The Targum reads 'the love of two women', meaning David's two wives. Radak's father read it as the strong love women have for husbands and sons.

sources.quote: מֵרְחִימַת תַּרְתֵּין נְשִׁין
sources.says: The Targum translates 'than the love of two women'.

sources.quote: ר"ל שתי הנשים שהיו לו לדוד אביגיל ואחינועם
sources.says: Radak explains the Targum as David's two wives, Abigail and Ahinoam, and gives his father's reading of women's love for husband and children.

1:27.headline: The lost 'weapons of war' are Saul and Jonathan
1:27.body: The lament ends with weapons lost. Rashi reads the weapons as Saul and Jonathan themselves, who were Israel's arms.

sources.quote: שָׁאוּל וִיהוֹנָתָן, שֶׁהָיוּ כְּלֵי זַיִן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says the weapons of war are Saul and Jonathan, who were the arms of Israel.

sources.quote: כל כך נפלו גבורי' כאלו אבדו כלי מלחמתם
sources.says: Radak gives two readings: so many warriors fell that it is as if their weapons were lost, or the weapons are Saul and Jonathan.

11:1.headline: Spelled 'messengers', but read as 'kings' going to war
11:1.body: The word is spelled like מלאכים, messengers, but the season meant is when kings go out to war. Radak says the extra aleph does not change the meaning, and the Targum and Malbim read 'kings'.

sources.quote: לעת צאת המלאכים. האלף נוספת
sources.says: Radak says the aleph in this word is an added letter.

sources.quote: לְעִדַן מִפַּק מַלְכַיָא
sources.says: The Targum translates 'at the time when kings go out'.

sources.quote: כי היה בחדש סיון שכל מלכי ארץ יוצאים
sources.says: Malbim says it was the month of Sivan, when all the kings of the earth go out to war, so David should have gone too.

11:4.headline: 'Making herself holy' here means finishing her purification
11:4.body: מתקדשת usually means becoming holy. Here commentators read it as purifying: she had just bathed at the end of her monthly impurity.

sources.quote: מתקדשת. רוצה לומר מטהרת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means purifying.

sources.quote: להודיע כי לא שכב עמה והיא נדה
sources.says: Radak says the verse tells us she had already purified herself, so the sin was with a married woman and not with a woman in her impurity.

11:8.headline: 'Wash your feet': rest from the road, or go to your wife?
11:8.body: David tells Uriah to go home and wash his feet. Metzudat David says this is a polite way to say sleep with your wife. Malbim reads it plainly: Uriah came in dusty from the road.

sources.quote: הוא כנוי לתשמיש המטה
sources.says: Metzudat David says washing the feet is a polite term for marital relations.

sources.quote: כי בא לפני המלך באבק שעל רגליו כבא מן הדרך
sources.says: Malbim says Uriah came before the king with dust on his feet from the road.

11:8.headline: A meal from the king's table, or a torch?
11:8.body: A משאת from the king follows Uriah out. Most read it as a portion of food. Ralbag also suggests a torch to light his way home.

sources.quote: כתרגומו סעודתא דמלכא
sources.says: Radak follows the Targum: a meal from the king.

sources.quote: ואפשר שיהיה מענין אבוקה ללותו בבואו אל ביתו
sources.says: Ralbag says it may instead be a torch sent to walk him home.

11:11.headline: Calling Joab 'my lord' before the king
11:11.body: Uriah calls Joab 'my lord' in front of David. The sages saw this as rebellion against the king, which is one way they explain his death.

sources.quote: שהיה לו לומר ועבדך יואב ועבדי אדוני
sources.says: Malbim cites the sages that Uriah should have said 'your servant Joab', and that this made him liable as a rebel.

11:21.headline: Gideon's name, with 'shame' put in place of Baal
11:21.body: Gideon is usually called Yerubaal. Here the name is Yerubbeshet: בשת, shame, is a name for the idol Baal that Gideon fought.

sources.quote: שֶׁעָשָׂה מְרִיבָה עִם הַבֹּשֶׁת, הוּא הַבַּעַל
sources.says: Rashi says this is Gideon, who fought the 'shame', which is Baal.

sources.quote: הוא ירובעל, וכאשר ׳בעל׳ גם ׳בושת׳ המה כנויי עבודה זרה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says he is Yerubaal, and both 'Baal' and 'shame' are names for idol worship.

11:21.headline: Here רכב is not a chariot but a millstone
11:21.body: רכב usually means a chariot. Here it is the upper stone of a mill, which a woman threw down on Abimelech.

sources.quote: הוא האבן העליונה מהרחים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רכב is the upper millstone, as in the law about millstones in Deuteronomy.

sources.quote: פַלְגוּת רֶכֶב רֵחַיָא
sources.says: The Targum translates 'a piece of the upper millstone'.

11:26.headline: She heard her 'man' died, but mourned her 'husband'
11:26.body: The verse first calls Uriah her איש, then her בעל. Malbim says איש is a word of love and בעל a word of ownership. He reads the switch as a hint that she was already divorced.

sources.quote: אבל היא ספדה על בעלה לא על אישה כי כבר היתה מגורשת
sources.says: Malbim says she mourned him as 'husband' and not as 'her man', because she was already divorced.

13:8.headline: She took 'the dough' before it was dough
13:8.body: Tamar takes the בצק and only then kneads it. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it is called dough for what it will become, since flour is only called dough after kneading.

sources.quote: אמר הבצק על שם סופו כי הקמח אחר שנלוש יקרא בצק
sources.says: Radak says it is named for its end, since flour is called dough only after it is kneaded.

sources.quote: העיסה, ואמר כן על שם סופו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is called dough by what it would become.

13:13.headline: 'He will not keep me from you': could they marry?
13:13.body: Tamar says the king would let Amnon marry her. Rashi says she was allowed to him, since her mother conceived her as a foreign captive; Ralbag adds that she objected to the act outside marriage, not to a forbidden match.

sources.quote: שמתרת אני לך, לפי שנתעברה בי אמי כשהיא נכרית יפת תאר
sources.says: Rashi says she was permitted to him, since her mother conceived her while a foreign captive.

sources.quote: אך אמרה שלא יעשה כן בישראל לבא על אשה דרך זנות אם לא יהיה דרך אישות
sources.says: Ralbag says she meant that in Israel one does not take a woman outside of marriage.

13:18.headline: A striped robe, like Joseph's
13:18.body: The word פסים is used for Joseph's coat and for Tamar's robe. Metzudat Zion says it was embroidered in bands a palm wide; Ralbag says the bands were of different colors.

sources.quote: פסים. מרוקמת ברוחב פס יד, וכן (בראשית לז ג): ועשה לו כתונת פסים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it was embroidered the width of a palm, as with Joseph's coat in Genesis 37.

sources.quote: לכוש מצבעים מתחלפים היה דרך משל כשיעור פסת יד מצבע אחד
sources.says: Ralbag says it was a garment of changing colors, each band about a palm wide.

13:18.headline: Robe or tunic? Why she was thrown out shamed
13:18.body: Malbim says a כתונת is the under-garment and a מעיל the robe on top, and Tamar was sent out without her robe. Metzudat David says both words name the same garment here.

sources.quote: שהכתונת הוא התחתון והמעיל יעטפו בו מלמעלה על כל הבגדים
sources.says: Malbim says the kutonet is the inner garment and the me'il is wrapped over all the clothes.

sources.quote: ויוצא אותה משרתו החוץ מופשטת ממעיל ובזויה מכבודה
sources.says: Malbim says the servant put her out stripped of her robe and shamed.

sources.quote: מעילים. היא כתונת פסים, וענינם אחד
sources.says: Metzudat David says the me'ilim are the striped tunic, and they are one thing.

13:20.headline: Absalom shrinks his brother's name: Aminon, not Amnon
13:20.body: Absalom says אמינון, not אמנון. Metzudat Zion says speakers add letters to make something small, and Radak calls it a way of showing contempt.

sources.quote: דרך המדברים להוסיף אותיות להקטין הדבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says speakers add letters to make a thing small, like ishon, 'little man' of the eye.

sources.quote: האמינון. דרך בזיון
sources.says: Radak says it is said in contempt.

13:25.headline: Vayifrotz: letters swapped from vayiftzar, 'he pressed him'
13:25.body: Metzudat Zion and Radak say ויפרץ is ויפצר, 'he urged', with two letters switched. Metzudat Zion says it means coaxing with many words.

sources.quote: ענין הפתוי ברבוי דברים, והוא הפוך מן (שם יט ג): ויפצר בם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means persuading with many words, and is ויפצר with letters reversed.

sources.quote: ויפרץ. כמו הפוך ויפצר
sources.says: Radak says vayifrotz is like vayiftzar reversed.

14:1.headline: Was David's heart toward Absalom, or against him?
14:1.body: לב המלך על אבשלום can mean the king's heart went out to Absalom or was set against him. Metzudat David says David felt warmly toward him, while Malbim says he still held a grudge, so Joab dared not ask him outright.

sources.quote: הכיר בהמלך אשר לבו טוב על אבשלום
sources.says: Metzudat David says Joab saw that the king's heart was kindly toward Absalom.

sources.quote: ידע יואב שעדיין לב המלך על אבשלום, רצה לומר שנוטר עליו איבה
sources.says: Malbim says Joab knew the king's heart was still against Absalom, holding a grudge, so he did not dare ask for him himself.

14:2.headline: Why Tekoa? The sages say olive oil made its people wise
14:2.body: Rashi and Radak cite the Talmud: olive oil was common in Tekoa, so wisdom was common there too. Radak adds that Tekoa was called 'alpha for oil', the best oil town in the land.

sources.quote: כִּי שֶׁמֶן זַיִת מָצוּי שָׁם, לְכָךְ חָכְמָה מְצוּיָה שָׁם
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: olive oil was common there, so wisdom was common there.

sources.quote: וכן אמרו תקוע אלפא לשמן ר״ל העיר המשובחת בשמן בארץ ישראל היתה תקועה
sources.says: Radak says Tekoa was called 'alpha for oil', meaning it was the city most praised for oil in the Land of Israel.

14:2.headline: A 'wise' woman here means a clever, crafty one
14:2.body: Maimonides says חכמה has four senses in Hebrew, and one is cleverness and cunning. He gives this verse as his example: a woman skilled in craft and trickery.

sources.quote: והוא מציין תחכום וערמה
sources.says: Maimonides says one of the four senses of the word is cleverness and cunning.

sources.quote: כלומר בעלת תחכום וערמה
sources.says: Maimonides cites 'he took from there a wise woman' and says it means a woman of cleverness and cunning.

sources.quote: ר״ל יודעה לסדר דבריה בחכמה ובשכל
sources.says: Ralbag says she knew how to arrange her words with wisdom and good sense.

14:3.headline: If Joab gave her the words, why did he need a wise woman?
14:3.body: Radak says Joab gave her only the outline, so she needed wisdom to answer the king herself. Malbim says the opposite: Joab guessed each reply the king would make and taught her what to say.

sources.quote: אם הוא סדר את המשל בפיה מה היה צריך לאשה חכמה לפי שתדע להשיב בחכמה למה שאמר לה המלך
sources.says: Radak asks why a wise woman was needed if Joab set the parable in her mouth, and answers that she had to reply wisely to what the king said, which Joab could not know.

sources.quote: כי יואב שער בדעתו מה שישיב לה המלך, ולמדה מה שתשיב היא על דבריו
sources.says: Malbim says Joab worked out what the king would answer and taught her what to reply.

14:5.headline: 'I am a widow, and my husband died': why say both?
14:5.body: A widow's husband is dead by definition. Radak says she means that if they kill her last son it will feel as though her husband died today, and Metzudat David says a mourner repeats her lament.

sources.quote: אבל עתה אחשוב שמת אישי היום אם יהרגו בני הנשאר לי
sources.says: Radak says she means she has been a widow for some time, but now she will feel her husband died today if they kill her remaining son.

sources.quote: גם זה מדרך אלמנה, תקונן ותכפיל דברי יללותה
sources.says: Metzudat David says this too is a widow's way, to lament and repeat her cries.

14:6.headline: An odd grammar hint: both brothers struck each other
14:6.body: The verb ויכו already has 'him' built in, and then the verse names the victim again. Malbim says this doubling means each brother hit the other and one died, so the dead one was also an attacker, just as Amnon had wronged Absalom.

sources.quote: ורצה לומר שזה הכה לזה וזה הכה לזה, והאחד המית, באופן שחברו היה כרודף כי הכהו גם כן
sources.says: Malbim says it means each struck the other and one killed, so the other was like a pursuer, since he struck too.

sources.quote: ושגם אמנון הכה אותו במה שעינה ובייש את אחותו
sources.says: Malbim says this matches Absalom's case, since Amnon had also struck him by violating and shaming his sister.

sources.quote: הכנוי טרם ההודעה וכן וישנו את טעמו
sources.says: Radak says the pronoun comes before the noun it refers to, as in other verses.

14:9.headline: 'The guilt is on me' politely means 'the guilt is on you'
14:9.body: Rashi and Radak say she meant the reverse, out of respect: if her son is killed, the guilt is the king's. Metzudat David reads it plainly: if her story proves false, the guilt for misleading him is hers.

sources.quote: בהפוך רצתה לומר אלא שכנתה לכבוד המלך כלומר עליך יהיה העון
sources.says: Radak says she meant the opposite but softened it for the king's honor: the guilt would be on him if her son were killed.

sources.quote: כִּנּוּי הוּא לִכְבוֹדוֹ, כְּלוֹמַר אַתָּה מַדְחֶה אוֹתִי
sources.says: Rashi says it is a polite turn for the king's honor: you are pushing me off, and if my son is killed, on whom is the guilt?

sources.quote: ואם יודע לאחר זה שלא כן הוא, אזי יהיה העון עלי על שהטעיתי את המלך
sources.says: Metzudat David says she meant that if it later proved untrue, the guilt would be hers for misleading the king.

14:11.headline: Many avengers, more bloodshed, or the Torah's long road?
14:11.body: Ralbag reads it as stopping the avengers from destroying more, since the surviving son is their kin too, and Radak says there were many avengers. Rashi, following the Targum, links it to 'the road is long' in Deuteronomy: God cared about the distance so a killer could escape.

sources.quote: ר״ל שלא ירבו גואלי הדם לשחת כי אין זה מחק גואלי הדם כי זה הנשאר הוא ג״כ קרובם
sources.says: Ralbag says it means the avengers should not add more destruction, since this is not their right when the survivor is also their relative.

sources.quote: כלומר שהיו רבים גואלים הדם ואם יצוה המלך לאחד יבא האחר ויהרגנו
sources.says: Radak says there were many avengers, so if the king warned one, another would come and kill him, which is why she wanted an oath.

sources.quote: שֶׁהִקְפִּיד עַל אֹרֶךְ הַדֶּרֶךְ לְהַצִּיל נְפָשׁוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says God was careful about the length of the road in order to save lives, as in Deuteronomy 19:6.

14:13.headline: 'Like one guilty', or 'like a slip of the tongue'
14:13.body: Targum Jonathan reads כאשם as 'like a guilty man'. Metzudat Zion and Radak read it as an error: while Absalom stays in exile, the king's oath to save her son looks like a slip.

sources.quote: וּמְמַלֵיל מַלְכָּא פִתְגָמָא הָדֵין כִּגְבַר חַיָב
sources.says: Targum Jonathan renders it 'the king speaks this word like a guilty man'.

sources.quote: כאשם. ענין שגגה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means an error.

sources.quote: אם דבר המלך הדבר הזה באשם ובשוגג דבר אותו שהרי הוא אינו משיב אבשלום
sources.says: Radak says people will think the king spoke in error, since he does not bring back Absalom, who also killed his brother.

14:14.headline: God does not 'lift' a soul: from death, or by bribe?
14:14.body: Rashi says God does not lift anyone out of death, and Radak says He shows no one favor, since all must die. Targum Jonathan reads it as the true Judge taking no bribe.

sources.quote: וְלֹא יִשָּׂא אֱלֹהִים נֶפֶשׁ. אִישׁ מִן הַמִּיתָה
sources.says: Rashi says God does not lift any man out of death.

sources.quote: כלומר לא ישא פני כל איש כי כלנו נמות
sources.says: Radak says it means God shows no one special favor, for all of us will die.

sources.quote: לֵית אֶפְשַׁר לְדַיָנָא דְקוּשְׁטָא לְקַבָּלָא מָמוֹן דִשְׁקַר
sources.says: Targum Jonathan renders it 'the true Judge cannot accept a false payment'.

14:14.headline: Who devises plans so the banished are not cast off?
14:14.body: Radak says it means God, who set laws so a killer is not put to death without witnesses. Rashi, and Radak's second reading, make it the king, who should plan so that one death does not lead to two.

sources.quote: אלהים חשב מחשבות ושם משפטים לבלתי ידח ההורג ויש לפרש וחשב מחשבות על המלך
sources.says: Radak says God devised plans and set laws so the killer would not be cast out, or else it refers to the king.

sources.quote: לְפִיכָךְ וְחָשַׁב הַמֶּלֶךְ מַחֲשָׁבוֹת
sources.says: Rashi reads it as the king: therefore let the king devise plans so that the banished one is not cast off.

14:21.headline: Written 'I have done', read 'you have done'
14:21.body: Radak found an exact text where it is written עשיתי, 'I have done', and read עשית, 'you have done'. Read that way, the king tells Joab: you set this up with the woman, so go and bring Absalom back.

sources.quote: ונסחא מדוייקת מצאתי כתוב עשיתי וקרי עשית
sources.says: Radak says he found an exact copy where it is written 'I have done' and read 'you have done'.

sources.quote: לשלח את התקועית, לזה לך והשיבו, כי המתחיל בדבר עליו לגמרו
sources.says: Metzudat David says Joab sent the woman, so he should go bring Absalom back, since whoever starts a thing must finish it.

14:30.headline: Written 'I will burn it', read 'go burn it'
14:30.body: Radak says the written form means Absalom himself would go with them to set the fire. The form read aloud is an order to the servants, and Radak says both come to the same thing.

sources.quote: הכתוב הוא על דרך נחי הפ״א למדבר בעדו ר״ל שהוא עצמו ילך עמהם והקרי הוא על דרך חסרי הפ״א והוא צווי לרבים
sources.says: Radak says the written form speaks of himself, meaning he would go with them, and the form that is read is a command to many, and both mean one thing.

15:1.headline: Fifty runners before him: a king's show, and a strange tradition
15:1.body: Running men before a chariot were a sign of a king. Ralbag says this was a big step for Absalom, who was not king. Rashi passes on a tradition that the fifty had their spleens removed and the soles of their feet carved.

sources.quote: הנה היה הענין הזה דבר גדול בחק אבשלום כי לא היה מלך
sources.says: Ralbag says this was a great thing for Absalom, since he was not a king.

sources.quote: כֻּלָּם נְטוּלֵי טְחוֹל, וַחֲקוּקֵי כַּפּוֹת רַגְלַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says all of them had their spleens removed and the soles of their feet carved.

15:2.headline: 'Which town are you from?' hid a jab at the king
15:2.body: Absalom asked each man where he came from. Metzudat David says this showed warmth. Malbim says it also hid a slur: that the king only cared for his own tribe.

sources.quote: הוא מדרך חיבה, לשאול את האדם מקומו וענינו
sources.says: Metzudat David says asking a man where he is from and about his affairs is a way of showing affection.

sources.quote: וגם הסתיר בדבריו מלשינות אחרת במה ששאל מאיזה עיר הוא כאומר שהמלך לא ישקוד רק על טובת שבטו
sources.says: Malbim says the question hid a slander, as if the king looked after only his own tribe.

15:4.headline: 'To me' or 'against me'? Absalom's odd little word
15:4.body: Absalom says ועלי, which usually means 'upon me' or 'against me', where 'to me' is expected. Radak says על often stands for 'to'. Malbim says it hints that even a man with a case against Absalom himself would be found right.

sources.quote: ועלי יבא. כמו ואלי ורבים על במקום אל
sources.says: Radak says ועלי means 'to me', and that על often stands in place of אל.

sources.quote: כיון במ"ש ועלי (תחת ואלי) שגם אם עליו יבא איש בריבו יצדיקנו
sources.says: Malbim says he chose ועלי instead of ואלי to hint that even if a man came against him in a dispute, he would rule for him.

15:4.headline: Would Absalom make everyone win, or judge them fairly?
15:4.body: והצדקתיו can mean 'I would declare him right'. Malbim asks how anyone can promise that, since one side must lose. He answers that it means the man who has the law on his side. Radak follows the Targum: 'I would judge him truly'.

sources.quote: ואיך אמר שהוא יצדיק כל איש אשר לו ריב ומשפט שזה אי אפשר, כי בהכרח יהיה אחד חייב ואחד זכאי
sources.says: Malbim asks how he could say he would vindicate everyone, since one party must be guilty and one innocent.

sources.quote: רצה לומר שהמשפט אתו בריבו
sources.says: Malbim says it means the man whose case is in the right.

sources.quote: והצדקתיו. כתרגומו ואדינניה בקושטא
sources.says: Radak says it means as the Targum puts it: 'I would judge him with truth'.

15:7.headline: Forty years since what? The verse does not say
15:7.body: The verse says 'at the end of forty years' but not from when. Rashi and Radak say it counts from when Israel first asked Samuel for a king. Malbim cites another view: near the end of David's forty-year reign.

sources.quote: שֶׁשָּׁאֲלוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מֶלֶךְ מִשְּׁמוּאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says it is forty years from when Israel asked Samuel for a king.

sources.quote: אמרו רז"ל ארבעים שנה מזמן ששאלו להם מלך
sources.says: Radak cites the Sages: forty years from the time they asked for a king.

sources.quote: ומהרי"א פי' ארבעים שנה של מלכות דוד
sources.says: Malbim cites a commentator who reads it as forty years of David's reign.

15:7.headline: Why Hebron? It is where David was first made king
15:7.body: Absalom said he had a vow to pay in Hebron. Radak and Ralbag say he picked it because David's kingship began there. Rashi cites the Sages, who say he went to bring fine sheep from Hebron.

sources.quote: לפי שהיה דעתו למרות ולמלוך בחר המקום שהוקם בו אביו למלך
sources.says: Radak says that since he meant to rebel and rule, he chose the place where his father was made king.

sources.quote: מפני שראה אבשלום ששם צמחה המלוכה לדוד והצליח בה חשב שיהיה המקום גורם
sources.says: Ralbag says Absalom saw that David's kingship began there and thought the place itself would bring success.

sources.quote: לְהָבִיא כְּבָשִׂים מֵחֶבְרוֹן, כִּי שָׁם הָיוּ כְּבָשִׂים שְׁמֵנִים
sources.says: Rashi cites the Sages: he went to bring sheep from Hebron, where the sheep were fat.

15:8.headline: Written 'bring me back', read 'let me dwell'
15:8.body: The word written here and the word read aloud differ. Radak says the written ישיב means 'bring back', and the spoken ישוב means 'settle': if God lets me live in Jerusalem.

sources.quote: ישיב כתיב וקרי ישוב ישיב לשון תשובה והקרי ישוב לשון ישיבה
sources.says: Radak says ישיב is written and ישוב is read; the first means returning, the second means dwelling.

15:12.headline: A plot is a 'knot' of men tied together
15:12.body: קשר means a knot or a tie. Metzudat Zion says a revolt is called this because the rebels tie themselves into one band.

sources.quote: המרד, על שם שבעלי המרד יתקשרו באגודה אחת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the revolt, named so because rebels bind themselves into one group.

15:14.headline: The Sages hear a doomed city and a rinsed cup
15:14.body: הדיח means 'push' or 'bring down' harm. Radak cites the Sages, who hear in it the doomed city, עיר הנדחת. They also hear rinsing a cup: once punishment starts, it does not stop until the cup is scoured.

sources.quote: והדיח. מלשון דחיה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from pushing.

sources.quote: ובדרש שלא ידון אותנו כעיר הנדחת ועוד אמרו נטל בעל הכוס להדיח את הכוס אינו זז עד שימרקנו
sources.says: Radak cites a midrash: so he will not judge us like the doomed city; and once the cup's owner starts rinsing it, he does not stop until he scours it.

15:17.headline: The 'Far House': a far place, or people keeping away
15:17.body: Beit HaMerchak means 'the far house'. Rashi and Radak follow the Targum: a place far from Jerusalem. Radak also cites a midrash that people shunned David and kept away from him.

sources.quote: בֵּית הַמֶּרְחָק. (תרגום:) ״בַּאֲתַר דְּרָחִיק״
sources.says: Rashi gives the Targum: 'in a far place'.

sources.quote: כלומר מקום שהיה רחוק מירושלם, ובדרש מלמד שנדוהו הה"ד ישובו לי יראיך מלמד שפרשו ממנו
sources.says: Radak says it was a place far from Jerusalem, and cites a midrash that it teaches people shunned David and separated from him.

15:18.headline: Pelethites: slingers, or judges who explain hard cases?
15:18.body: The Targum calls the Pelethites slingers. Ralbag takes them as the high court. He ties the name to יפלא, a case 'too hard' for lower judges, which the court explains.

sources.quote: וְכָל קַשָׁתַיָא וְכָל קַלְעַיָא
sources.says: The Targum renders them 'all the archers and all the slingers'.

sources.quote: והם גם כן מבארים כל מה שיפלא למשפט באיזה דבר שיהיה מדברי התורה
sources.says: Ralbag says they also explain any legal matter of Torah that is too hard to decide.

15:19.headline: Fleeing David calls Absalom 'the king'
15:19.body: David tells Ittai to go back and stay 'with the king'. Rashi and Metzudat David say he means Absalom, who has now made himself king.

sources.quote: עִם הַמֶּלֶךְ. עִם אַבְשָׁלוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says 'with the king' means with Absalom.

sources.quote: על אבשלום יאמר, שמלך עתה
sources.says: Metzudat David says he is speaking of Absalom, who has now become king.

15:24.headline: 'Poured out' the ark? Here it means set it down
15:24.body: ויצקו looks like 'they poured'. Rashi and Radak say it means they set the ark in place. Metzudat Zion says it is like ויציגו, since the letters ג and ק can swap.

sources.quote: וַיַּצִּקוּ. כְּמוֹ וַיַּצִּיגוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like ויציגו, 'they set up'.

sources.quote: והוא כמו ויציגו, כי אותיות גיכ״ק מתחלף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like ויציגו, because the letters ג, י, כ, ק interchange.

sources.quote: ויציקו. כמו ויעמידו
sources.says: Radak says it means 'they stood it up'.

15:24.headline: Abiathar 'went up', or stepped down from the priesthood?
15:24.body: Read plainly, Abiathar went off to one side with the ark. Rashi and Radak cite the Sages: that day he left the high priesthood, because he asked the Urim and Tummim and got no answer.

sources.quote: לפי פשט הכתוב יראה כי פי' ויעל אביתר נסתלק לצד אחד עם הארון
sources.says: Radak says by the plain reading Abiathar moved to one side with the ark.

sources.quote: אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם נִסְתַּלֵּק מִן הַכְּהוּנָּה, שֶׁשָּׁאַל בָּאוּרִים וְתוּמִּים וְלֹא נַעֲנָה
sources.says: Rashi says that day he was removed from the priesthood, because he asked the Urim and Tummim and was not answered.

15:27.headline: 'Do you see?' or 'You are a seer'
15:27.body: Rashi reads הרואה as a question: do you see this is good advice? The Targum reads it as 'you are a seer', a prophet. Radak explains: the holy spirit rested on Zadok that day.

sources.quote: אִם רוֹאֶה אַתָּה שֶׁעֵצָה נְכוֹנָה הִיא
sources.says: Rashi says it means: if you see that this is sound advice.

sources.quote: וַאֲמַר מַלְכָּא לְצָדוֹק כַּהֲנָא חֶזְוַיָא אַתְּ
sources.says: The Targum has the king tell Zadok the priest, 'you are a seer'.

sources.quote: כלומר נביא אתה שראה ששרתה עליו רוח הקדש ונענה אותו היום באורי' ותומים
sources.says: Radak says the Targum means 'you are a prophet', since David saw the holy spirit on Zadok, who was answered that day through the Urim and Tummim.

15:28.headline: Written 'the crossings', read 'the plains' of the wilderness
15:28.body: The written word means the crossings, by the Kidron stream. The word read aloud means the open plains of the wilderness. Radak says both fit, but the read one fits better.

sources.quote: כן כתיב וקרי בערבות ופי' הכתוב בעבר נחל קדרון ופי' הקרי כתרגומו במשרי מדברא ושניהם נכונים בענין אלא שהקרי יותר קרוב
sources.says: Radak says the written form means across the Kidron, the read form means the wilderness plains, and both are right, though the read form is closer.

15:31.headline: Not 'David told', but 'David was told'
15:31.body: Read word by word, the verse says David told. Rashi and Radak say a small letter ל is missing. It means the messenger told David.

sources.quote: וּלְדָוִד הִגִּיד הַמַּגִּיד
sources.says: Rashi says it means the messenger told David.

sources.quote: חסר למ"ד השמוש ופי' ולדוד הגיד המגיד
sources.says: Radak says the prefix ל is missing, so it means the messenger told David.

15:31.headline: Make the advice foolish, or make it look foolish?
15:31.body: David prays: סכל Ahithophel's advice. Rashi says it means 'spoil' it. Metzudat David gives two readings: keep him from advising wisely, or make Absalom think his advice is foolish.

sources.quote: סַכֶּל. קַלְקֵל, כְּמוֹ (קהלת י:יד): ״הַסָּכָל יַרְבֶּה דְבָרִים״
sources.says: Rashi says סכל means 'spoil', as in 'the fool multiplies words'.

sources.quote: סכל עצתו לבל ייעץ בחכמה. או רצה לומר: שיתן בלב אבשלום, לחשוב אשר עצת אחיתופל היא עצה סכלה
sources.says: Metzudat David says either that God make him advise unwisely, or that God make Absalom think the advice is foolish.

17:1.headline: Ahitophel says 'David', not 'King David'
17:1.body: Ahitophel offers to chase 'after David' and leaves out the title king. Radak brings the sages: this was contempt, because of what David did with Bathsheba. They say she was Ahitophel's granddaughter.

sources.quote: ובזהו בדבריו שאמר אחרי דוד ולא אמר אחרי המלך דוד מפני המעשה שעשה בבת שבע
sources.says: Radak says Ahitophel scorned David by saying 'after David' and not 'after King David', because of what David did with Bathsheba.

sources.quote: ואמרו כי בת שבע היתה בת בנו של אחיתופל
sources.says: Radak brings the teaching that Bathsheba was the daughter of Ahitophel's son.

17:4.headline: The plan seemed 'straight', not 'good'
17:4.body: The verse says the plan was ישר, straight, in their eyes, not that it pleased them. Malbim says killing the king still felt wrong to them. They only saw that the plan led straight to its goal.

sources.quote: לא כתב וייטב הדבר, כי באמת היה דבר זה רע בעיניהם להרוג את המלך, רק שמצאו שהיא עצה ישרה
sources.says: Malbim says the verse does not say the thing pleased them, because killing the king was bad in their eyes. They only found it a straight plan.

17:10.headline: Who is the lion-hearted man who will melt?
17:10.body: Rashi reads 'he' as any listener, even a brave one, who hears of a first defeat. Radak reads it as Ahitophel himself: Hushai praises him as lion-hearted, then says even he would lose heart.

sources.quote: וְאוֹתוֹ הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ אֲפִלּוּ הוּא בֶּן חַיִל
sources.says: Rashi says it means the one who hears the news, even if he is a brave man.

sources.quote: פי' והוא אחיתופל שהוא בן חיל שאמר אבחרה נא שנים עשר אלף
sources.says: Radak says 'he' is Ahitophel, the brave man who offered to pick twelve thousand.

sources.quote: שבחו כדי שלא יראה כי כדי לגנותו הוא מדבר
sources.says: Radak says Hushai praised him so it would not look like he was speaking to put him down.

17:12.headline: Not 'and we' but 'we will land on him'
17:12.body: ונחנו looks like the word for 'we'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as a verb: we will come down and camp on him, like dew settling on the ground.

sources.quote: וְנָנוּחַ עָלָיו, לְשׁוֹן חֲנִיָּה
sources.says: Rashi says it means we will settle on him, from the word for camping.

sources.quote: ונחנו. מלשון חניה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the word for camping.

17:13.headline: Ropes to drag a city, or bands of troops?
17:13.body: Radak reads חבלים as ropes: Israel is so many they could drag a whole city into the valley. Rashi follows the Aramaic, 'camps', since חבל can mean a band of people, as in 'a band of prophets'.

sources.quote: שאפילו ירימו חבלים אל העיר למשכה ולסחבה עד הנחל
sources.says: Radak says they could even raise ropes to the city to drag it down to the valley.

sources.quote: (תרגום:) ״מַשִׁרְיָן״, כְּמוֹ ״חֶבֶל נְבִיאִים״
sources.says: Rashi says the Aramaic translation has 'camps', like 'a band of prophets'.

17:25.headline: Called 'the Israelite' here and 'the Ishmaelite' in Chronicles
17:25.body: Amasa's father Yitra is 'the Israelite' here, but 'the Ishmaelite' in Chronicles. Radak and Metzudat David say he was an Israelite who lived in the land of Ishmael.

sources.quote: ישראל היה אלא שגר בארץ ישמעאל
sources.says: Radak says he was an Israelite who lived in the land of Ishmael.

sources.quote: ובדברי הימים (א ב יז) אמר הישמעאלי, לפי שהתגורר בארץ ישמעאל
sources.says: Metzudat David says Chronicles calls him the Ishmaelite because he lived in the land of Ishmael.

17:25.headline: Jesse is called 'Serpent' because he died without sin
17:25.body: Abigail is 'daughter of Nahash', but she was David's sister, Jesse's daughter. The sages say Jesse is called נחש, serpent, because he never sinned. He died only because of the serpent in Eden.

sources.quote: שֶׁמֵּת בְּלֹא עָוֹן, בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says Nahash is Jesse, who died without sin, through the serpent's counsel.

sources.quote: ויתכן לומר, שנולדה מאשת ישי מבעלה הראשון, ושמו נחש
sources.says: Metzudat David also suggests she was born to Jesse's wife from an earlier husband named Nahash.

17:27.headline: Is this the Ammonite king's son, now loyal to David?
17:27.body: Shobi son of Nahash brings David food. Rashi says he is Hanun son of Nahash, the Ammonite king who once shamed David's men. Radak finds that hard and says he was an Israelite living in Rabbah.

sources.quote: וְשֹׁבִי בֶן נָחָשׁ. הוּא חָנוּן בֶּן נָחָשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says Shobi son of Nahash is Hanun son of Nahash.

sources.quote: והדרש שאומר כי הוא חנון בן נחש מלך בני עמון רחוק הוא
sources.says: Radak says the midrash that he is Hanun, the Ammonite king, is far-fetched.

sources.quote: ישראל היה והיה גר ברבת בני עמון אחר שכבשה דוד
sources.says: Radak says he was an Israelite living in Rabbah after David captured it.

17:28.headline: A bed, or a jug for pouring?
17:28.body: משכב usually means a bed. Radak first reads it as a vessel for pouring water on the hands, from שכבת הטל, a layer of dew. He also brings those who read it as a bed.

sources.quote: כלי ששופכין ממנו לידים, משכב לשון שפיכה וכן ותעל שכבת הטל
sources.says: Radak says it is a vessel for pouring onto the hands, since משכב means pouring, as in a layer of dew.

sources.quote: וי"מ מטה ונקראת משכב לפי ששוכב אדם עליה
sources.says: Radak brings others who say it is a bed, called משכב because a person lies on it.

18:3.headline: Help us from the city, or pray that God helps us
18:3.body: The word is written one way and read another. Read aloud, it means 'to help'. Radak says the written form means 'to bring help', that is, to pray to God to help them. The Targum also has David pray for them from the city.

sources.quote: וכתיב לעזיר ביו"ד וקרי לעזור בוי"ו והקרי מבואר והכתיב מבנין הפעיל להעזיר והוא יוצא לשלישי פי' שתעזיר אתה אותנו על ידי האל כלומר שתתפלל לאל שיעזרנו
sources.says: Radak says the read form is plain, while the written form means that you cause help to reach us through God, that is, pray to God to help us.

sources.quote: וּכְעַן טָב אֲרֵי תְצַלֵּי עֲלָנָא מִן קַרְתָּא לְמִסְעַד
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum: it is better that you pray for us from the city to help.

18:5.headline: 'Gently with the boy', or 'shelter the boy for me'
18:5.body: לאט is a rare word. Metzudat Zion and Radak say it means 'gently': do not come at Absalom in anger. Ralbag reads it as 'hide' or 'shelter': save the boy for my sake.

sources.quote: ענין נחת, כמו (בראשית לג יד): אתנהלה לאטי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means gently, as in Jacob's 'I will go along gently'.

sources.quote: ופי' לאט בנחת כלומר לא תבואו בכעס וברוגז להכותו
sources.says: Radak says it means gently: do not come at him in anger to strike him.

sources.quote: ר"ל להסתיר בעבורי לזה הנער שתמלט אותו אם יבא לידך
sources.says: Ralbag says it means to hide the boy for my sake, and rescue him if he falls into your hands.

18:6.headline: Why Ephraim's forest was on the wrong side of the Jordan
18:6.body: Ephraim's land was west of the Jordan, but this battle is east of it. Rashi and Radak explain: Joshua let every tribe graze in any forest. Ephraim grazed its herds here, so the forest took its name.

sources.quote: וּמֵהֵיכָן הָיָה יַעַר לְאֶפְרַיִם בְּעֵבֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן מִזְרָחָה
sources.says: Rashi asks how Ephraim could have a forest east of the Jordan.

sources.quote: וְהָיוּ מַרְעִין שָׁם בְּהֵמוֹתֵיהֶם, הָיָה נִקְרָא יַעַר אֶפְרָיִם
sources.says: Rashi says they grazed their animals there, so it was called the forest of Ephraim.

sources.quote: היא שיהיו מרעין בהמותיהם בחורשין
sources.says: Radak says one of Joshua's rules was that tribes could graze their animals in any forest.

18:8.headline: Written 'scattered men', read 'the scattered battle'
18:8.body: The written form is plural and the spoken form is singular. Radak says the written one means the fighters scattered across the forest. The spoken one means the battle as a whole spread out.

sources.quote: הכתוב נפצות לשון רבות והקרי נפוצת לשון יחידה והכתיב אומר על הגבורים והגדודים מזה ומזה שהיו נפוצים על פני כל היער והקרי אומר בכלל על המלחמה
sources.says: Radak says the written plural speaks of the fighters scattered over the forest, and the read singular speaks of the battle as a whole.

18:8.headline: The forest 'ate' more men than the sword
18:8.body: The verse says the forest devoured more than the sword. Rashi follows the Targum: the wild beasts of the forest. Radak adds that it may mean the trees themselves, which wounded the men as they fled.

sources.quote: חַיּוֹת רָעוֹת שֶׁבַּיַּעַר, כֵּן תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן
sources.says: Rashi says it means the wild beasts in the forest, as the Targum renders it.

sources.quote: ויתכן לפרש היער עצמו שהיו נפוצים ונפצעים בעצי היער בברחם
sources.says: Radak says it may mean the forest itself: they scattered and were wounded by its trees as they fled.

18:9.headline: A word found only here: the tangle of branches
18:9.body: שובך appears only here. Metzudat Zion says it is the same as סובך, a thicket, as in the ram caught in the thicket. It is named for branches that tangle into each other.

sources.quote: כמו סובך בסמ״ך, והוא ענין ענף, כמו (שם כב יג): בסבך בקרניו ויקרא כן על שם שנאחזים ומסובכים זה בזה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like סובך with a samekh, meaning branches, as with the ram in the thicket, named because they grip and tangle together.

sources.quote: סוכת העץ מסתבכת ענף בענף נקראת שובך
sources.says: Radak says the tree's canopy, tangled branch in branch, is called a שובך.

18:9.headline: Caught by the head: the Sages say by his proud hair
18:9.body: The verse says his head caught in the oak. Radak says he had much hair, and cites the Sages: he was proud of his hair, so he hung by it. Rashi cites the Sages that he drew his sword to cut it and saw hell open beneath him.

sources.quote: ונאחז בו ראש אבשלום שהיה לו שיער רב ואמרו רז"ל לפי שנתגאה בשערו נתלה בשערו
sources.says: Radak says Absalom's head, with its thick hair, caught in it, and the Sages said he was proud of his hair so he was hanged by it.

sources.quote: שָׁלַף חַרְבּוֹ לָקוּץ שְׂעָרוֹ, וְרָאָה גֵּיהִנֹּם פְּתוּחָה תַּחְתָּיו
sources.says: Rashi cites the Sages: he drew his sword to cut his hair and saw Gehinnom open beneath him.

18:12.headline: Written 'I would not', read 'even if'
18:12.body: The written word is ולא, 'and not': I would not take a thousand pieces of silver. The word read aloud is ולו, 'even if': even if a thousand were weighed into my hands. Radak gives both.

sources.quote: ולא כתיב כלומר לא הייתי לוקח אלף כסף בדבר הזה ואתה אמרת שהיית נותן לי עשרה כסף והקרי הוא ולו
sources.says: Radak says the written ולא means 'I would not take a thousand silver for this, and you offered ten', and the read form is ולו.

sources.quote: ולו אנכי. ואם אנכי, וכן (שופטים ח יט): לו החייתם אותם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ולו means 'and if', as in 'if you had let them live'.

18:13.headline: Written 'against his life', read 'against my own life'
18:13.body: The written word says 'his life': killing Absalom would be a lie against him. The word read aloud says 'my life': I would be lying against myself, since the king forbade it. Radak gives both.

sources.quote: בנפשו כתיב פי' בנפשו של אבשלום אם הייתי הורג אותו שקר הייתי עושה בעצמו כי המלך צוה עליו והקרי הוא בנפשי כלומר אפילו לא יודע הדבר הייתי עושה שקר בעצמי
sources.says: Radak says the written form means against Absalom's life, and the read form means against myself, even if no one found out.

18:14.headline: Joab will not plead, or Joab will strike first?
18:14.body: אחילה is an unusual word. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as 'plead': I will not keep asking you. Malbim reads it as 'begin': I will start the killing myself, so the sin is on me.

sources.quote: לֹא אֲבַקֵּשׁ עוֹד בַּקָּשָׁה מִמְּךָ, כִּי אֲנִי אֵלֵךְ
sources.says: Rashi says it means: I will not ask you again, I will go myself.

sources.quote: אבקש, כמו (מלכים ב ה ג): אחלי אדוני
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'I will ask', as in 'would that my lord'.

sources.quote: לא אתה תכהו רק אוחילה לפניך אני אתחיל להכותו, בענין שיהיה החטא עלי
sources.says: Malbim says it means: you will not strike him, I will begin to strike him, so the sin is on me.

18:14.headline: Three darts for the three hearts Absalom stole
18:14.body: Radak says these were thin spears, called שבטים, 'rods'. He cites the Sages: Absalom stole three hearts, his father's, the court's and Israel's, so three darts went into his heart.

sources.quote: ולהב בראשיהם כמו חניתות היו אלא שהדקי' נקראו שבטים
sources.says: Radak says they had blades at their tips like spears, but thin ones are called שבטים.

sources.quote: ואמרו רז"ל לפי שגנב ג' לבבות לבב אביו ולבב בית דין ולב אנשי ישראל לפיכך נתנו בו ג' שבטים
sources.says: Radak cites the Sages: because he stole three hearts, his father's, the court's and Israel's, three darts were put into him.

18:17.headline: 'Each to his tent', spelled singular: they fled alone, ashamed
18:17.body: The word for 'his tents' is spelled without the letter that marks the plural. Radak cites a midrash: the rebels were ashamed, so they did not band together. Each one fled alone.

sources.quote: חסר כתיב בלא יו"ד הרבים ויש בו דרש לפי שהיו נכלמי' מן המרד שעשו לא התחברו יחד אלא כל אחד נס לאהלו
sources.says: Radak says it is written without the plural yod, and a midrash says they were ashamed of the revolt, so they did not gather but each fled to his tent.

18:18.headline: A missing letter worth ten years of Absalom's life
18:18.body: 'In his life' is spelled without a yod, a letter worth ten. Radak cites a midrash: ten years were taken from Absalom's life because he lay with his father's ten concubines.

sources.quote: ויש בו דרש כי חסרו חיי אבשלום עשר שנים על ששכב עם עשר פלגשי אביו לפיכך חסר יו"ד שהוא בחשבון עשרה
sources.says: Radak cites a midrash that ten years were cut from Absalom's life for lying with his father's ten concubines, so a yod, worth ten, is missing.

18:18.headline: 'I have no son', though Absalom had three sons
18:18.body: Earlier the book says Absalom had three sons. Radak says they must have died. He also cites the Sages: whoever burns another man's grain leaves no son, and Absalom burned Joab's field.

sources.quote: ולמעלה כתיב ויולדו לאבשלום שלשה בנים ובת אחת היו לו אלא שמתו
sources.says: Radak says that earlier it says Absalom had three sons and a daughter, but they died.

sources.quote: גמירי שכל השורף תבואתו של חבירו אינו מניח בן ליורשו והוא שרף תבואתו של יואב
sources.says: Radak cites the Sages' tradition that one who burns another's grain leaves no son to inherit, and Absalom burned Joab's grain.

18:20.headline: A word read but not written: he died 'rightly'
18:20.body: כן is read aloud here but not written. With it, Joab says: because the king's son is dead, this is no news for you. Radak cites a midrash that reads כן as 'rightly': Absalom died justly, for rebelling against his father.

sources.quote: כן קרי ולא כתיב והקרי הוא יותר קרוב כאלו אמר כי על אשר בן המלך מת אין אתה ראוי לבשר ויש בו דרש כי ע"כ ועל יושר מת שמרד באביו
sources.says: Radak says כן is read but not written, meaning 'since the king's son died, you should not bring the news', and a midrash reads it as 'rightly he died, for rebelling against his father'.

sources.quote: כִּי עַל אֲשֶׁר בֶּן הַמֶּלֶךְ מֵת, לְפִיכָךְ לֹא טוֹבָה לְךָ הַבְּשׂוֹרָה זֹאת
sources.says: Rashi says: because the king's son died, this news is not good for you to bring.

18:28.headline: God 'shut in' the rebels: Ahimaaz picks a careful word
18:28.body: סגר usually means 'shut'. Metzudat Zion says here it means 'handed over'. Malbim says Ahimaaz chose it on purpose. 'God judged your enemies' would have hinted Absalom was dead.

sources.quote: סגר. מסר, כמו (עמוס א ו): להסגיר לאדום
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means handed over, as in 'to hand them over to Edom'.

sources.quote: אחימעץ נשמר ולא אמר בלשון שרצה להגיד (בפסוק י"ט) כי שפטו ה' מיד אויביו, שבזה ירמוז מיתת אבשלום, רק אמר אשר סגר את האנשים
sources.says: Malbim says Ahimaaz took care not to say 'God judged him from his enemies', which would hint at Absalom's death, and said only 'who handed over the men'.

18:29.headline: 'Peace to the boy', or 'Is the boy safe?'
18:29.body: David says שלום לנער, 'peace to the boy'. Metzudat David says it is a question: is the boy safe? Malbim says David first said it hopefully, because Ahimaaz's words made it seem Absalom was alive.

sources.quote: שלום. כמו השלום, ובלשון שאלה אמר
sources.says: Metzudat David says שלום here is like השלום, said as a question.

sources.quote: השלום לנער, תחלה אמר שלום, כי ממ"ש אחימעץ, היה נראה לו שאבשלום חי
sources.says: Malbim says David first said שלום because from Ahimaaz's words it seemed Absalom was alive.

19:1.headline: David cries 'my son' eight times, and the sages counted them
19:1.body: In this verse and verse 5, David cries בני, my son, eight times over Absalom. Rashi brings the sages' reading: seven cries lifted Absalom out of seven levels of Gehinnom, and the eighth brought him to the world to come.

sources.quote: שְׁמוֹנֶה פְּעָמִים, אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages that the eight cries of 'my son' raised Absalom from seven levels of Gehinnom and brought him to the world to come.

sources.quote: כן דרך הנוהים לכפול דבריהם
sources.says: Radak says mourners repeat their words, and also brings the teaching about the eight times.

19:1.headline: Malbim hears 'he went up' as 'he lifted him up'
19:1.body: ויעל plainly says David went up to the room over the gate. Malbim also reads it as 'he raised up': by his weeping David lifted Absalom out of the gates of Gehinnom.

sources.quote: שהעלהו משערי גיהנם בבכייתו
sources.says: Malbim reads ויעל as a verb done to someone else, so that David raised Absalom from the gates of Gehinnom by his weeping.

20:1.headline: Not 'was called' but 'happened to be there'
20:1.body: נקרא usually means 'was called'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as 'happened to be there', from מקרה, chance. The Aramaic translation says the same: a wicked man chanced to be there.

sources.quote: וְשָׁם נִקְרָא. נִזְדַּמֵּן
sources.says: Rashi says the word means 'happened to be present'.

sources.quote: נקרא. מלשון מקרה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from מקרה, a chance event.

sources.quote: וְתַמָן אִתְעַרַע גְבַר רַשִׁיעָא
sources.says: The Aramaic translation says 'and there a wicked man chanced to be'.

20:3.headline: Widows while their husband was still alive
20:3.body: David shut away the ten concubines Absalom had taken, and they lived as 'living widows' until they died. Radak, following the Aramaic, says they were widows though their husband lived. Ralbag says no other man could take them, since they were the king's.

sources.quote: כתרגומו מתקרין עד יום מותן ארמלן דבעליהן קיים
sources.says: Radak quotes the Aramaic: they were called widows until their death, though their husband was alive.

sources.quote: הנה זה קרא להן בעבור היותן פילגשי המלך ואין ראוי לאחר להשתמש בהן
sources.says: Ralbag says they were called this because they were the king's concubines and no one else could have them.

20:7.headline: David's guards: archers and slingers, or families of judges?
20:7.body: The Aramaic translation renders the כרתי and פלתי as 'archers and slingers'. Ralbag says they were two families from whom the high court came in David's day.

sources.quote: וְקַשָׁתַיָא וְקַלְעֲיָא
sources.says: The Aramaic translation calls them archers and slingers.

sources.quote: הם שני משפחות שזכרנו שהיו מהם הסנהדרין בימי דוד
sources.says: Ralbag says they were two families from whom the Sanhedrin came in David's time.

20:14.headline: Two letters swapped, same word, as with כבש and כשב
20:14.body: The word is written ויקלהו but read ויקהלו, 'they gathered'. Radak says Hebrew often has the same word with two letters swapped, like כבש and כשב, 'lamb', or שמלה and שלמה, 'garment'.

sources.quote: ושניהם א' כי מלים שוים באותיות הפוכות רבי' במקרא כמו כבש וכשב שמלה ושלמה
sources.says: Radak says both forms mean the same, since Scripture has many words whose letters are swapped, like כבש and כשב, שמלה and שלמה.

20:15.headline: A low outer wall, or an army ringing the city?
20:15.body: The Aramaic translation reads חל as an army: troops surrounded the city. Rashi brings another view: חל is the outer wall, which fell while the inner wall held. Metzudat David says it is the low wall in front of the high one.

sources.quote: וְאַקְפָהּ מַשִׁרְיָן
sources.says: The Aramaic says 'and surrounded it with camps'.

sources.quote: הִפִּילוּ הַחוֹמָה הַחִיצוֹנָה, וְנִתְחַזְּקָה לַעֲמֹד עַל יְדֵי הַפְּנִימִית
sources.says: Rashi brings a view that they knocked down the outer wall, and the city held by its inner wall.

sources.quote: והיא החומה הנמוכה שאצל הגבוה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is the low wall next to the high one.

20:20.headline: Why Joab says 'far be it' twice
20:20.body: Rashi says one 'far be it' is for Joab himself and one is for the king. Metzudat Zion says the word is doubled because the idea was so foreign to him.

sources.quote: חָלִילָה לִי, חָלִילָה לַמֶּלֶךְ
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'far be it from me, far be it from the king'.

sources.quote: וכפל המלה לרוב הזרות אצלו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is doubled because the thing was so strange to him.

20:21.headline: 'Against the king, against David': either alone is a capital crime
20:21.body: Rashi brings a midrash on the doubled phrase. Rebelling against a king deserves death even if he is not David. Rebelling against David deserves death even if he were not king. All the more so against both.

sources.quote: בַּמֶּלֶךְ אֲפִלּוּ אֵינוֹ דָוִד, חַיָּב מִיתָה, וּבְדָוִד אֲפִלּוּ אֵינוֹ מֶלֶךְ, חַיָּב מִיתָה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בַּמֶּלֶךְ בְּדָוִד
sources.says: Rashi says rebelling against a king, even not David, or against David, even not king, deserves death, and all the more so both.

21:1.headline: 'Because of Saul': his sin, or a wrong done to him?
21:1.body: Rashi and Metzudat David read 'because of Saul' as a wrong done to Saul: he was buried in a hurry, in secret, and never mourned as a king should be. The famine was for that, and for the Gibeonites.

sources.quote: על עון שאול שנקבר פתאום בהחבא
sources.says: Rashi says it was for the sin over Saul, who was buried suddenly and in hiding.

sources.quote: על העון הנעשה בשאול שלא נספד לפי כבודו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it was for the wrong done to Saul, who was not mourned as his honor deserved.

21:1.headline: Saul 'killed the Gibeonites', though no story tells of it
21:1.body: The Bible never tells of Saul killing Gibeonites. Rashi says some were killed with the priests of Nob, where they worked, and the sages add that killing the priests who fed them counts as killing them.

sources.quote: כשהרג נוב עיר הכהנים, המית מהם שבעה
sources.says: Rashi says when Saul killed Nob, the city of priests, he killed seven of them.

sources.quote: מתוך שהרג את הכהנים שהיו מספיקין להם מזון, העלה עליו הכתוב כאלו המיתם
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages that since he killed the priests who supplied their food, Scripture counts it as if he killed them.

sources.quote: מתי המית שאול את הגבעונים
sources.says: Malbim asks when Saul killed the Gibeonites.

21:2.headline: 'Not of the children of Israel': a people who would not forgive
21:2.body: Rashi says the Gibeonites showed cruelty, while Israel is marked by mercy, shame and kindness. Radak brings the sages: whoever will not be appeased is not of Israel.

sources.quote: שלשה סימנים יש באומה זו, רחמנים ובישנים וגומלי חסדים
sources.says: Rashi says this nation has three signs: merciful, modest and doing kindness.

sources.quote: כל שאינו מקבל פיוס אינו מבני ישראל
sources.says: Radak cites the sages that anyone who will not accept appeasement is not of Israel.

21:4.headline: Written 'I', read 'we': each Gibeonite refused alone
21:4.body: The word is written לי, 'to me', but read לנו, 'to us'. Rashi and Radak say David tried to pay each Gibeonite in private, and each one answered 'I want no silver'.

sources.quote: אמר שמא הם מתבישין זה מזה, הלך ופיס כל אחד ואחד לעצמו, ולא נתפיסו
sources.says: Rashi says David thought they were ashamed before each other, so he tried each one alone, and none agreed.

sources.quote: וכל אחד אמר לו אין לי כסף וזהב עם שאול ועם ביתו
sources.says: Radak says each one told him, 'I have no claim of silver or gold on Saul'.

21:6.headline: 'Saul, chosen of God': who said it?
21:6.body: Plainly, God had chosen Saul as king. The sages say the Gibeonites did not say these words; a voice from heaven did, showing Saul's sins were forgiven.

sources.quote: שהאל בחרו למלך, ובדרש הם לא אמרו בחיר ה' אלא בת קול יצתה ואמרה בחיר ה'
sources.says: Radak says God chose him as king, and the midrash says a heavenly voice, not the Gibeonites, said 'chosen of the Lord'.

sources.quote: בת קול יצאה ואמרה: בחיר ה׳
sources.says: Rashi says a heavenly voice went out and said 'chosen of the Lord'.

21:7.headline: David 'spared' Mephibosheth: pity, or gladness?
21:7.body: Rashi says David prayed that the Ark would not pick Mephibosheth when the sons passed before it. Rav Saadia reads ויחמל as 'was glad': Mephibosheth was only a child and took no part in the killing.

sources.quote: בקש רחמים שלא יקלטנו הארון, שהעבירם לפני הארון
sources.says: Rashi says David prayed the Ark would not take him, since he passed them before the Ark.

sources.quote: פי' רב סעדיה גאון וישמח כי מפיבשת לא היה מן ההורגים כי קטן היה
sources.says: Radak cites Saadia that it means David was glad, since Mephibosheth was a small child and not among the killers.

21:8.headline: 'Michal's five sons', though Michal had no children
21:8.body: Michal never had children, and Adriel was her sister Merab's husband. Rashi, Radak and Ralbag say Merab bore the sons and Michal raised them, so they are called hers.

sources.quote: אלא מירב ילדה, ומיכל גדלה, לפיכך נקרא על שמה
sources.says: Rashi says Merab bore them and Michal raised them, so they are named after her.

sources.quote: שהרי אמר במה שקדם ומיכל בת שאול לא היה לה ולד עד יום מותה
sources.says: Ralbag notes Scripture said Michal had no child to the day of her death.

sources.quote: וית חמשת בני מרב דרביאת מיכל
sources.says: The Targum says 'the five sons of Merab, whom Michal raised'.

21:9.headline: Written 'sevenfold', read 'the seven of them'
21:9.body: The written form שבעתים means 'sevenfold', but it is read שבעתם, 'the seven of them'. Radak says the written form was taken to mean twice seven, because none of them left children.

sources.quote: ביו"ד כתיב ר"ל שתי פעמים שבעה כמו שבעתים יוקם קין
sources.says: Radak says it is written with a yod, meaning twice seven, as in 'Cain will be avenged sevenfold'.

sources.quote: והקרי הוא שבעתם ר"ל הם השבעה
sources.says: Radak says the read form means 'the seven of them'.

21:10.headline: Rizpah on the rock, and the Rock whose work is perfect
21:10.body: Plainly she spread sackcloth on the rock where the bodies hung. Radak brings a midrash that she said 'the Rock, His work is perfect', accepting God's judgment.

sources.quote: ובדרש מה ותטהו לה אל הצור שאמרה הצור תמים פעלו שהצדיקה עליה את הדין
sources.says: Radak cites the midrash that she said 'the Rock, His work is perfect', accepting the judgment.

sources.quote: הצור. הסלע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says hatzur means the rock.

21:16.headline: Yishbi-benob: a giant who 'came about Nob'?
21:16.body: Metzudat Zion and Radak say this was simply his name. Radak also brings a midrash reading it as 'a man who came over Nob', paying David back for the priests killed there, and calls it far-fetched.

sources.quote: ובדרש ישבי בנוב איש שבא על עסקי נוב
sources.says: Radak cites the midrash that Yishbi-benob means a man who came on account of Nob.

sources.quote: וכל זה רחוק
sources.says: Radak says all of this is far-fetched.

sources.quote: וישבי בנוב. כן היה שמו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says that was his name.

21:16.headline: Keino: a weapon named nowhere else
21:16.body: Metzudat Zion says it is a weapon with no other match in the Bible. Radak ties it to Arabic, where a spear shaft is called al-qana; Ralbag guesses it is the spearhead, named like a nest for the socket the shaft fits into.

sources.quote: קינו. שם כלי זיין, ואין לו חבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the name of a weapon and has no partner word.

sources.quote: הוא עץ החנית וכן נקרא בערבי עץ החנית אלקנה
sources.says: Radak says it is the spear shaft, which in Arabic is called al-qana.

sources.quote: אחשוב שקרא קינו להבת החנית וקראו קן מצד הנקבות שבו אשר בו יכנס עץ החנית
sources.says: Ralbag thinks it is the spearhead, called a nest for the hole the shaft goes into.

21:16.headline: Harafah: 'the giant', or a mother named Orpah?
21:16.body: Metzudat Zion and Radak say הרפה means the giant, one of the Rephaim. Rashi and Radak also bring the midrash that it is the name of the giants' mother, and Rashi calls them the four sons of Orpah.

sources.quote: הרפה. הענקה, כמו (שם יד ה): ויכו את רפאים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says harafah means the giant, as with the Rephaim.

sources.quote: וכבר כתבנו דעת הדרש למעלה שהוא שם האם
sources.says: Radak says the midrash takes it as the mother's name.

sources.quote: לצרף מיתת ארבעה בני ערפה
sources.says: Rashi speaks of the death of the four sons of Orpah.

21:16.headline: Girded with 'something new': a new sword, and a first battle
21:16.body: The verse does not say what was new. Radak and Metzudat David say a new sword; Rashi heard it was his first day in armor, when fighters try to win a name.

sources.quote: והוא חגור חדשה. חרב חדשה
sources.says: Radak says it means a new sword.

sources.quote: שאותו היום נתחנך ללבוש כלי מלחמה, ודרך המחנכים לעשות נצחון וגבורה ביום חנוכם
sources.says: Rashi says he heard that this was his first day in armor, and new fighters try to win a victory that day.

21:19.headline: Elchanan killed Goliath? Some say Elchanan is David
21:19.body: Rashi and the Targum say Elchanan is David. Radak follows Chronicles: Elchanan killed Goliath's brother, and David killed Goliath; he admits he does not know why David would be called Elchanan.

sources.quote: אלחנן. דוד
sources.says: Rashi says Elchanan is David.

sources.quote: וקטל דוד בר ישי
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'and David son of Jesse killed'.

sources.quote: והוא אחיו הרגו אלחנן בגוב וגלית הרגו דוד באפס דמים
sources.says: Radak says Elchanan killed Goliath's brother at Gob, and David killed Goliath at Ephes-dammim.

sources.quote: אבל מה שקרא דוד אלחנן לא ידעתי לו טעם
sources.says: Radak says he does not know a reason to call David Elchanan.

21:19.headline: 'Son of Ya'arei-oregim': a family of weavers
21:19.body: Oregim means weavers. Rashi and Radak say the family wove the curtain for the Temple, and Radak says the Temple is called ya'ar, 'forest'.

sources.quote: שהיו משפחתו אורגים פרכת למקדש הקרוי יער
sources.says: Rashi says his family wove the curtain for the Sanctuary, which is called ya'ar.

sources.quote: קרא ישי יערי לפי שהיה אורג פרוכות הצריכות לבית המקדש ובית המקדש נקרא יער
sources.says: Radak says Jesse was called Ya'arei because he wove curtains for the Temple, which is called ya'ar.

sources.quote: והיה ממשפחת אורגים רצה לומר משפחת בצלאל ראש האורגים
sources.says: Malbim says he was of a family of weavers, the family of Bezalel.

21:20.headline: Ish madon: a very tall man, or a man of quarrels?
21:20.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read מדון from מדה, measure: a man of great height, as Chronicles says איש מדה. Ralbag reads it from מדון, strife: a man of fights and war.

sources.quote: ובדברי הימים (דברי הימים א יא:כג) כתיב: ״איש מדה״, כלומר גבוה מאד
sources.says: Rashi says Chronicles writes 'a man of measure', meaning very tall.

sources.quote: מדון. מלשון מדה, ורוצה לומר בעל מדה גדולה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from measure, meaning a man of great size.

sources.quote: איש מדון. ר"ל איש בעל ריב ומלחמה
sources.says: Ralbag says it means a man of strife and war.

21:20.headline: Six and six, twenty-four: why count the fingers twice?
21:20.body: Rashi and Radak say 'six and six' alone could mean six on both hands together, and '24' alone could mean seven on one hand and five on the other. Saying both makes it six on each.

sources.quote: ואילו אמר כ"ד ולא אמר שש ושש הייתי אומר ה' באחת ושבע באחת לכך נאמר שש ושש
sources.says: Radak says with only '24' we might think five on one and seven on the other, so it says 'six and six'.

sources.quote: שלא תאמר אצבעות שתי ידיו אינן אלא שש
sources.says: Rashi says '24' is needed so you do not think both hands together had only six.

22:1.headline: Saul is one of 'all his enemies', so why name him?
22:1.body: Rashi says Saul is named on his own because he was David's fiercest enemy and pursuer. Radak says Saul weighed as much as all his other enemies together.

sources.quote: וַהֲלֹא שָׁאוּל בַּכְּלָל הָיָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁהָיָה אוֹיְבוֹ וְרוֹדְפוֹ מִכֻּלָּם
sources.says: Rashi says Saul was included among the enemies, but is named because he was the greatest enemy and pursuer of them all.

sources.quote: ואמר ומכף שאול כי הוא היה שקול כנגד כל אויביו
sources.says: Radak says Saul is named because he was equal to all David's enemies together.

22:5.headline: 'Torrents of wickedness', or sicknesses?
22:5.body: נחלי usually means streams or torrents. Rashi reads it as enemy troops sweeping in like a flood. Metzudat Zion reads it from חולי, sickness.

sources.quote: גְּיָסוֹת שׁוֹטְפוֹת כְּנַחַל
sources.says: Rashi says it means troops sweeping in like a torrent.

sources.quote: נחלי. מלשון חולי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from sickness.

22:6.headline: 'Cords of Sheol': birth pains, or a band of the wicked?
22:6.body: חבלי can mean pains, like a woman in labor, or a band of people, like 'a band of prophets'. Metzudat Zion and Radak read pains. Rashi follows the Targum: a camp of the wicked surrounded him.

sources.quote: ענין כאב מן חבלי יולדה ויונתן תרגם משרית רשיעין כמו חבל נביאים
sources.says: Radak says it means pain, as in labor pains, while the Targum reads 'a camp of the wicked', as in 'a band of prophets'.

sources.quote: כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ: ״מַשְׁרִית״
sources.says: Rashi follows the Targum, which reads it as a camp.

sources.quote: חבלי. מכאובי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means my pains.

22:9.headline: Smoke from His nose: why אף means both nose and anger
22:9.body: אף means nose, and also anger. Rashi says this is why: an angry person snorts and breathes out hot air, like smoke from the nostrils.

sources.quote: וְזֶהוּ כָּל לְשׁוֹן חֲרוֹן אַף, שֶׁהָאַף נוֹחֵר וּמַעֲלֶה הֶבֶל
sources.says: Rashi says this is the source of every phrase of 'burning nose' for anger: the nose snorts and gives off vapor.

sources.quote: שעל ידי חמום הכעס, נראה כעין עשן יוצא מנחירי האף
sources.says: Metzudat David says the heat of anger looks like smoke coming out of the nostrils.

22:11.headline: God does not fly: the cherub does, and it means speed
22:11.body: Maimonides warns not to read this as God flying. He says the cherub is what flies, and the picture shows how fast the rescue came.

sources.quote: כי הכרוב הוא אשר עף, והכוונה במשל הזה היא מהירות בואו של הדבר ההוא
sources.says: Maimonides says it is the cherub that flies, and the figure means the speed of what was coming.

sources.quote: ודימה נשיבת הרוח, לעפיפת כנפי העוף
sources.says: Metzudat David says the verse compares the blowing wind to the beating of a bird's wings.

22:30.headline: Run at a troop, or crush it?
22:30.body: ארוץ looks like 'I run'. Radak says it may come from רצץ, to crush: with God I break an enemy troop. Or it means I run toward them without fear. Ralbag reads 'I break'.

sources.quote: וארוץ משרש רצץ
sources.says: Radak says ארוץ may come from the root רצץ, to crush.

sources.quote: או פי' ארוץ לקראת גדוד אויבי ולא אירא מהם
sources.says: Radak says it may instead mean I run toward the enemy troop without fear.

sources.quote: ארוץ גדוד. אשבר וארוץ חיל רב
sources.says: Ralbag says it means I break and crush a large army.

22:42.headline: Not 'they were saved' but 'they looked for help'
22:42.body: ישעו looks like the word for saving. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it means turning to look: the enemies turned to God for help, and no one saved them. Rashi says the verse must be read out of order.

sources.quote: הֲרֵי זֶה מִקְרָא מְסֹרָס
sources.says: Rashi says the verse is out of order: they turned to God, He did not answer, and there was no savior.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ יִפְנֶה
sources.says: Rashi says ישעו means 'turn', as in Isaiah 17:7.

sources.quote: ישעו. ענין הפנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means turning toward.

23:2.headline: The spirit spoke 'in me', not 'to me'
23:2.body: Rashi says prophecy is called speech because the spirit enters the prophet and speaks from inside him. Maimonides places David's psalms at the level where a force comes on a person, awake, and moves him to speak praise and wisdom.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁהָרוּחַ נִכְנָס בּוֹ בְּקֶרֶב הַנָּבִיא, וּמְדַבֵּר בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the spirit enters into the prophet and speaks in him.

sources.quote: וכוח אחר מופיע עליו ומדובב אותו
sources.says: Maimonides describes a level where another force comes on a person and makes him speak, and says David wrote Psalms this way.

23:2.headline: Even the exact wording came from God
23:2.body: Malbim says the spirit can come on a poet in two ways: it can stir the subject while the poet picks his own words, or it can give the words too. With ומלתו על לשוני, David claims both.

sources.quote: אם רק לעוררו בכח אלהי על ענין השיר, והמלות והמליצה ידבר המליץ משכלו, או שגם המלות והמליצה יהיה ברוח ה'
sources.says: Malbim says the spirit either only stirs the poet to the subject while he picks the words himself, or the words too come from God; here it was both.

23:3.headline: God spoke 'to me', or spoke 'about me'?
23:3.body: Radak and Malbim read לי דבר as 'He spoke for my sake', a promise about David told to a prophet. Maimonides agrees that God made the promise through a prophet, such as Nathan.

sources.quote: ופירושו אמר לי דבר בעבורי ואמר ודבר לשמואל הנביא
sources.says: Radak says it means God spoke on David's behalf, telling the prophet Samuel.

sources.quote: משמעות הדברים היא שהוא הבטיח לו על ידי נביא, בין אם נתן או נביא אחר
sources.says: Maimonides says the verse means God promised David through a prophet, Nathan or another.

sources.quote: וכל לי ולו ולהם הסמוכים אצל דבור פי' בשביל ורצה לומר שדבר בשבילי
sources.says: Malbim says that 'to me' next to the verb for speaking means 'for my sake'.

23:3.headline: The righteous person who overrules even God
23:3.body: Plainly, the verse describes a just ruler. Rashi brings the sages' reading: God says 'I rule over people, and who rules over Me? The righteous: I make a decree and he cancels it.'

sources.quote: מוֹשֵׁל בָּאָדָם אֲנִי, וּמִי מוֹשֵׁל בִּי, צַדִּיק, שֶׁאֲנִי גּוֹזֵר גְּזֵרָה וְהוּא מְבַטְּלָהּ
sources.says: Rashi cites the rabbis: I rule over man, and the righteous rules over Me, for I decree and he cancels it. He says the plain reading comes first.

23:7.headline: Burned where they sit, or burned when they cease?
23:7.body: Radak reads בשבת as 'in their place', where the thorns grow. Metzudat Zion reads it as 'at their end', like 'the oppressor has ceased'. Rashi also reads it as God sitting on the throne of judgment.

sources.quote: או ישרפו אותם במקום שבתם כלומר במקום שהם צומחים
sources.says: Radak says they are burned in their place, where they grow.

sources.quote: בשבת. ענין בטול, כמו (ישעיהו יד ד): שבת נוגש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means ending, as in 'the oppressor has ceased'.

sources.quote: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא יוֹשֵׁב עַל כִּסֵּא הַדִּין
sources.says: Rashi says it refers to God sitting on the seat of judgment.

23:8.headline: The hero who 'sits in the seat': a scholar as well
23:8.body: Rashi reads ישב בשבת as one who sits in the high court. Ralbag hears שבת, rest: he rested from all other work to study wisdom.

sources.quote: יוֹשֵׁב בְּשֶׁבֶת סַנְהֶדְרִין
sources.says: Rashi says he sat in the seat of the Sanhedrin.

sources.quote: כי מרוב אהבתו החכמה היה שובת מכל מלאכה אחרת ומתעסק תמיד בקנין החכמה
sources.says: Ralbag says that out of love of wisdom he rested from all other work and always studied.

23:8.headline: Head of three gifts, or head of the officers?
23:8.body: Rashi reads ראש השלשי as first in three things: wisdom, looks and courage. Radak and Metzudat Zion read שלשי as officers, the king's picked men.

sources.quote: בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים הַלָּלוּ הוּא רֹאשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says he was first in three things.

sources.quote: השלשי. ענין גבורים ונכבדים, כמו (שמות יד ז): ושלשים על כלו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means mighty and honored men, as in 'officers over all of them'.

23:8.headline: Soft as a worm at study, hard as wood in war
23:8.body: The sages split the name עדינו העצני. עדינו sounds like 'soft and delicate': at his studies he curled up gently like a worm. העצני sounds like עץ, wood: in battle he was hard as timber.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה, כּוֹרֵךְ וּמְקַשֵּׁר עַצְמוֹ כְּתוֹלַעַת
sources.says: Rashi says that when he studied Torah he curled himself up like a worm, and when he went to war he was hard as wood.

sources.quote: בשעה שהיה עוסק בתורה מעדן עצמו כתולעת ובשעה שהיה יוצא למלחמה מקשה עצמו כעץ
sources.says: Radak gives the same reading from the rabbis, then says that plainly it is simply the hero's name.

23:9.headline: Risking their lives, or taunting the enemy?
23:9.body: Radak reads בחרפם like 'he risked his life': the three heroes threw themselves at the Philistines. The Aramaic translation reads it as the Philistines taunting Israel, and Ralbag as the heroes taunting the Philistines.

sources.quote: וענינו כמו חרף נפשו למות שענינו גלה
sources.says: Radak says it is like 'he risked his life to die', meaning they exposed themselves to danger.

sources.quote: כַּד חֲסִידוּ פְּלִשְׁתָּאֵי
sources.says: Targum Jonathan renders it 'when the Philistines taunted'.

sources.quote: ידמה שהם היו מחדפים בפלשתים להתפאר עליהם
sources.says: Ralbag says the heroes were taunting the Philistines and boasting over them.

23:11.headline: A pack like wild beasts, a crowd, or a raid for food?
23:11.body: חיה can mean a wild animal or a living thing. Rashi says the Philistines gathered as a troop, like wild beasts. Metzudat Zion says it means a crowd. Ralbag says they came to take food (מחיה) from the fields.

sources.quote: לַחַיָּה. לִגְדוּד כְּחַיּוֹת הַשָּׂדֶה
sources.says: Rashi says it means a troop, like wild animals of the field.

sources.quote: לחיה. רוצה לומר לעדה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a gathering.

sources.quote: ר"ל שכבר נאספו לקחת המחיה מהשדה
sources.says: Ralbag says they gathered to take the food from the field.

23:15.headline: Did David want water, or an answer to a legal question?
23:15.body: Plainly David was thirsty for the water of his home town. The sages read 'water' as Torah: he needed to ask the court that sat at Bethlehem's gate. Radak reports this reading and finds it strange.

sources.quote: הֻצְרַךְ לִשְׁאוֹל שְׁאֵלָה מִסַּנְהֶדְרִין הַיּוֹשְׁבִים בְּשַׁעַר בֵּית לָחֶם
sources.says: Rashi cites the rabbis: David needed to ask a question of the court sitting at the gate of Bethlehem.

sources.quote: והם פי' מי ישקני מים דרך משל כי המים הם התורה
sources.says: Radak says the rabbis read 'who will give me water' as a parable for Torah, and calls their reading surprising.

23:20.headline: Written 'a living man', read 'a valiant man'
23:20.body: The written text has חי, living; it is read חיל, valiant. Radak says the sages took the written word to mean Jehoiada was fully righteous, since the righteous are called living even after death.

sources.quote: ומה שכתוב חי דרשו בו שהיה צדיק גמור וצדיקים אפילו במיתתם קרואים חיים
sources.says: Radak says the rabbis read the written חי to mean he was fully righteous, since the righteous are called living even in death.

3:5.headline: Eglah, "calf": a pet name for Michal?
3:5.body: עגלה means a young cow. Rashi says this is David's loving name for Michal, as Samson called his wife "my calf". Radak adds that by the plain meaning Eglah was a different wife.

sources.quote: זו מיכל, שהיתה חביבה עליו, וכן הוא אומר (שופטים יד:יח): ״לולא חרשתם בעגלתי״
sources.says: Rashi says Eglah is Michal, who was dear to David, as in Samson's "had you not plowed with my calf".

sources.quote: ולפי הפשט יש לפרש עגלה זו אחרת
sources.says: Radak says that by the plain meaning this Eglah was another woman.

3:12.headline: "Whose is the land?" A question, or an oath?
3:12.body: Radak reads it as a question: who should have the land but you? Rashi and the Targum read it as an oath: by the One who owns the land.

sources.quote: למי ארץ.} לשון שבועה, במי שהארץ שלו
sources.says: Rashi says "whose is the land" is an oath: by the One whose land it is.

sources.quote: מקימנא במאן דעבד ארעא
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum: "I swear by the One who made the earth".

sources.quote: למי תאות הארץ אלא לך
sources.says: Radak reads it as: to whom does the land belong if not to you?

3:29.headline: A cane for bad legs, or a woman's spindle?
3:29.body: David curses Joab's house with one who "holds a פלך". Rashi reads it as leaning on a stick because of sick legs. Metzudat Zion and Malbim say a פלך is the spindle women spin with.

sources.quote: נשען על מקלו מחמת חולי הרגלים
sources.says: Rashi says it means one who leans on his stick because of a sickness in his legs.

sources.quote: והוא המטה שטוות בו הנשים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the rod women use for spinning.

sources.quote: שאין יודע להתפרנס רק ממטוה כנשים
sources.says: Malbim says it means a man who can earn a living only by spinning, like women.

3:35.headline: First to cut him down, then to feed him: one letter's difference
